title: One-Time Setup for Suite Synergy Integration and CSO API
subtitle: Making invisible operational cost legible with a service blueprint

slides.title: One-Time Setup for Suite Synergy Integration and CSO API
slides.standfirst: Forty-plus manual configuration tasks, absorbed by Professional Services and developers, collapsed into a single action — by first making the cost visible to the people who could authorise removing it.

bullets.text: Principal UX Designer, Sourcing and CSO
Service blueprinting, introduced to the product organisation
One-time setup, zero developer steps per customer

slides.notes: This is a design case about a screen almost nobody sees. Lead with that: the interesting part is how a cost that never reaches a feedback channel got onto a roadmap.

slides.title: Integration setup is invisible work
slides.standfirst: The cost was absorbed by Professional Services and by developers, not experienced by end users — so it never surfaced as a complaint, and never competed for roadmap space against things that did.

bullets.text: Time consumed manually enabling each customer's integration.
A developer had to perform several manual steps for every single customer who wanted CSO API access.
A suppressed number of joint Core + CSO customers actually ran integrated instances, because the setup burden deterred them.

callout.text: Not that the process was long. That nobody with authority over the roadmap could see it.

slides.notes: Three costs in three different budgets, which is exactly why no single owner was complaining. The third one is the commercial argument.

slides.title: Start with everyone in the system, not the user in front of you
slides.standfirst: Customers, users, Professional Services, developers, Operations — five stakeholder groups, only one of whom logs into the thing.
slides.notes: The reframe: the end user is not the person paying the cost, so a user-centred method aimed only at them would have found nothing.

slides.title: Desk research on the mechanics, then watching the process happen

bullets.text: CSO settings, endpoint authentication, endpoints, labels, commands and the process documentation.
Professional Services, walked through the live process alongside them rather than asked about it.
How comparable suites handled cross-product setup.
Mapped before anything was drawn, so the blueprint had lanes to fill.

figure.alt: Process diagram of the integration setup as it existed
figure.caption: The process diagram — the input to the blueprint, not the output

slides.notes: Walking through it live is the detail that matters. Asked to describe the process, people describe the documented one; watched, they show you the real one.

slides.title: A service blueprint was the only artefact that could show backstage cost
slides.standfirst: A user flow shows what the customer does. A blueprint shows what has to happen behind them for that to work — which is precisely where all the effort was hiding.

callout.text: The organisation had no format in which "a developer does this by hand for every customer" could appear next to "the customer clicks Save". Without one, the two costs were never compared.

slides.notes: This slide is the thesis of the case study. Service blueprinting became the standard functional design artefact for integration work afterwards, which is the real outcome.

slides.title: Six parallel lanes, from end user to Core backend
slides.standfirst: Redrawn here from the original. Each column is a stage of the setup; each row is a layer of the system that has to act for that stage to complete.

lanes.name: End user
steps: Asks for a Core + CSO integrated instance
Works across both products as one suite

lanes.name: PS / Ops / Support
steps: Receives the request and schedules the work
Sets up the OpenID Connect provider and links accounts
Configures company logo, Coupa Setup and colours, navigation menu

lanes.name: CSO team / backend
steps: A developer manually enables API access
Creates the API user and key

figure.caption: The bottom-left cell — "a developer manually enables API access" — is the whole business case

slides.notes: Walk it left to right along the PS lane, then drop into the bottom lane and stop. Point at the first cell of the CSO backend lane: that is a person, per customer, forever.

slides.title: One screen, one action, no developer
slides.standfirst: The end user's experience of forty tasks disappearing is a single confirmation. That asymmetry is what makes this work hard to fund and easy to justify afterwards.

bullets.text: Endpoint authentication, endpoints, labels and commands provisioned together.
API enablement no longer requires a member of the development team.
Professional Services time redirected from configuration to implementation.

slides.notes: If asked what the design work actually was: deciding what belongs in one action, what needs confirmation, and what has to fail safely — all of it derived from the blueprint.

slides.title: The numbers, and the artefact that outlived them

items.label: Configuration tasks collapsed into a single action
System layers mapped, end user through to Core backend
Developer steps per customer for API enablement
One-time setup replacing per-customer endpoint creation

callout.text: Service blueprinting became the standard functional design artefact for integration work across CSO and the core platform, and was applied again to suite synergy between supply chain and CSO.

slides.notes: End on the method spreading rather than the metric. One shipped screen is a project; a new artefact in the organisation's vocabulary is a change.

slides.title: You cannot remove a cost the organisation cannot see
slides.standfirst: The design work was collapsing forty tasks into one. The research work was finding a way to show product management that the forty existed.

bullets.text: Backstage and support cost, in one artefact

slides.notes: Likely question: how did you get PS to give you the time? Answer: they were the ones absorbing it, so the interview was the first time anyone had asked.
